title: What decimal number does each arrow show?
description: Two number lines are cut into ten equal parts, so the video divides each gap by ten to find the size of one part, then counts parts from the left end to read the decimal number at each arrow.
teaching_notes: One idea: divide the gap between the two end numbers by the number of equal parts to get the size of one part, then count parts from the left end. Ask the class how big one part is on the first line before any work is shown. Watch for students who read the second line as steps of zero point one.

source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q2
video_script.why: The child can divide a total by a count to get the amount for one, and now does the same to get the size of one part on a number line.
video_script.substitution: The gap between the two end numbers is divided by ten to get one part, and the parts are counted from the left end.
video_script.anchor: Two number lines: one from 3.1 to 3.2 and one from 2.15 to 2.17, each cut into ten equal parts, each with an arrow at the sixth mark after the left end
video_script.payoff_line: The arrows sit at three point one six and two point one six two

final_answer.spoken: three point one six and two point one six two

maths_rules: first line: 3.2 - 3.1 = 0.1, and 0.1 / 10 = 0.01 for one part
second line: 2.17 - 2.15 = 0.02, and 0.02 / 10 = 0.002 for one part
check: the middle mark of the second line is 2.15 + 5 x 0.002 = 2.16, and the arrow is one part after it
video_script.design: One idea: divide the gap by ten to get one part, then count parts from the left end. The two number lines stay on the board all video; the working band builds one line at a time in the idea part.
open_questions: The arrow place (the sixth mark after the left end) is taken from the worklist; the extracted book text does not show the figure.

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about two number lines.
<bookmark mark='first'/>The first runs from three point one to three point two, cut into ten equal parts.
<bookmark mark='firstarrow'/>Its arrow is at the sixth mark after three point one.
<bookmark mark='second'/>The second runs from two point one five to two point one seven, also in ten equal parts.
<bookmark mark='secondarrow'/>Its arrow is at the sixth mark after two point one five.
What decimal number is at each arrow?

beats.on_screen: a gap split into ten equal parts with one part lit; the words size of one part = gap ÷ number of parts

marks.split: a gap between two numbers is cut into ten equal parts
marks.rule: the words size of one part = gap ÷ number of parts are written

narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>The marks on a number line cut the gap between the two end numbers into equal parts.
<bookmark mark='one'/>To find one part, we divide the gap by the number of parts.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>It is the same idea as finding the price of one gram.

beats.on_screen: Given: line one from 3.1 to 3.2; line two from 2.15 to 2.17; each in 10 equal parts; each arrow at the 6th mark after the left end

marks.given: the two lines and their ends are written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, two lines, each cut into ten equal parts. Each arrow is at the sixth mark after the left end.

beats.on_screen: To find: the decimal number at each arrow

marks.find: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the decimal number at each arrow.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, line one: gap = 3.2 − 3.1 = 0.1; one part = 0.1 ÷ 10 = 0.01

marks.why: the step title and the first line are lit
marks.gap: 3.2 − 3.1 = 0.1 is written and the gap is shaded
marks.part: 0.1 ÷ 10 = 0.01 is written and one part is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step one, find the size of one part on the first line.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The gap is three point two minus three point one, which is zero point one.
<bookmark mark='part'/>Divide zero point one by ten. One part is zero point zero one.

marks.count: six parts are counted from 3.1 and shaded

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step two, the arrow is six parts after three point one.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Six parts of zero point zero one make zero point zero six.
<bookmark mark='add'/>The arrow is at three point one plus zero point zero six.

marks.why: the step title and the second line are lit
marks.gap: 2.17 − 2.15 = 0.02 is written and the gap is shaded
marks.part: 0.02 ÷ 10 = 0.002 is written and one part is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step three, find the size of one part on the second line.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The gap is two point one seven minus two point one five, which is zero point zero two.
<bookmark mark='part'/>Divide zero point zero two by ten. One part is zero point zero zero two.

marks.count: six parts are counted from 2.15 and shaded

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step four, the arrow is six parts after two point one five.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Six parts of zero point zero zero two make zero point zero one two.
<bookmark mark='add'/>The arrow is at two point one five plus zero point zero one two.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check line two: the 5th mark is the middle, 2.15 + 5 × 0.002 = 2.16; the arrow is one part after it

marks.mid: the fifth mark on the second line is lit
marks.after: the arrow is shown one part after the middle mark

narration: <bookmark mark='mid'/>Step five, check by another route. On the second line, the fifth mark is the middle.
<bookmark mark='val'/>Five parts of zero point zero zero two make zero point zero one. Add it to two point one five to get two point one six.
<bookmark mark='after'/>The arrow is one part after it, so it is a little more than two point one six.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The arrows sit at three point one six and two point one six two.
<bookmark mark='tie'/>The first number is on the first line, and the second is on the second line.
